- Both authored by William L. Benzon, part of his ongoing series of informal essays probing ChatGPT's internal structure through behavioral experiments rather than model internals
  - Shared method: black-box "reverse engineering" — inferring the shape of the model's learned representations purely from patterns in its outputs
- Reference paper ("ChatGPT tells stories...") examines narrative generation as a probe of internal structure
  - Looks at how the model organizes and sequences story elements, revealing latent schematic/associative structure
  - Frames this as evidence for how a language model encodes structured knowledge without symbolic rules
- Subject paper ("ChatGPT's Ontological Landscape") extends the same reverse-engineering stance to categorical/conceptual structure
  - Uses list-generation probes (e.g. "give me 20 things" chains, abstract-vs-concrete 20-questions tests) to surface how the model clusters and drifts between categories
  - Where the reference paper reverse-engineers narrative structure, the subject paper reverse-engineers ontological/category structure — two facets of the same underlying question: what kind of "world model" does the statistical patterning in ChatGPT implicitly encode?
- Together they form a paired case study
  - Story-telling paper: sequential/narrative organization
  - Ontological-landscape paper: categorical/conceptual organization
  - Both conclude that emergent, human-legible structure (plot patterns, category hierarchies) arises from next-token statistics without being explicitly programmed
